edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 1, Paris 1844), Apologeticus, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Augustus imperii formator, ne dominum quidem dici se volebat; et hoc enim dei est cognomen. Dicam plane imperatorem dominum, sed more communi, sed quando non cogor, ut dominum dei vice dicam. Caeterum liber sum illi; dominus enim meus unus est, Deus omnipotens et aeternus, idem qui et ipsius. Qui pater patriae est, quomodo dominus est. Sed est gratius nomen pietatis, quam potestatis; etiam familiae magis patres, quam domini vocantur. Tanto abest, ut imperator deus debeat dici, quod non potest credi non modo turpissima, sed et perniciosa adulatione; tanquam si habens imperatorem, alterum appelles, nonne maximam et inexorabilem offensam contrahes ejus, quem habuisti, etiam ipsi timendam, quem appellasti? Esto religiosus in deum, qui vis illum propitium imperatori. Desine alium Deum colere vel credere, atque ita et hunc deum dicere, cui deo opus est. Si non de mendacio erubescit adulatio ejusmodi, hominem deum appellans, timeat saltem de infausto. Maledictum est ante apotheosin deum Caesarem nuncupare.
pass_a_gloss: Augustus, the founder of the empire, did not even want to be called master; for this is also a surname of God. I will call the emperor master plainly, but in the common manner, and when I am not forced to say master in place of God. Meanwhile, I am free from him; for my master is one, God omnipotent and eternal, who is the same for him as well. He who is the father of the country, is master in this way. But the name of piety is more pleasing than that of power; even parents of families are called fathers rather than masters. So far is it from the case that the emperor ought to be called God, that it cannot be believed, not only a most shameful, but also a pernicious flattery; as if, having an emperor, you were to call another, would you not incur the greatest and most inexorable offense of him whom you have, and also one to be feared by him whom you called? Be devout to God, who wishes to make him favorable to the emperor. Cease to worship or believe in another God, and thus also call this one God, for whom God is needed. If such flattery does not blush at lying, calling a man God, let it at least fear the ill-omened. It is a curse to call Caesar God before his apotheosis.

pass_b_english: Augustus, the founder of the empire, did not even want to be called master, for that is a title of God as well. I will call the emperor master plainly, but in the common manner, and only when I am not forced to say 'master' in place of God. Meanwhile, I am free from him; for my master is one, God omnipotent and eternal, who is the same for him as well. He who is the father of the country is master in that sense. But the name of piety is more pleasing than that of power; even parents in families are called fathers rather than masters. It is so far from being the case that the emperor ought to be called God that it cannot be believed—it is not only a most shameful but also a pernicious flattery. It is as if, having an emperor, you were to call another 'master'; would you not incur the greatest and most inexorable offense of the one you already have, and also make the one you called an object of fear? Be devout toward God, if you wish to make Him favorable to the emperor. Cease worshiping or believing in another God, and thus also call this one God—the one for whom God is needed. If such flattery does not blush at the lie of calling a man God, let it at least fear the ill omen. It is a curse to call Caesar God before his apotheosis.
